contents.content:
The WBPSC Clerkship exam is one of the most popular government job exams in West Bengal, mainly because you only need to be Madhyamik pass to apply. The West Bengal Public Service Commission (WBPSC) holds it to fill Lower Division Clerk and Lower Division Assistant posts, along with other similar clerical posts, in the Secretariat, Directorates, District Offices and Regional Offices of the state government.

Because the qualification is basic, lakhs of candidates apply every time. That means the exam is not hard in terms of difficulty level, but it is tough in terms of competition. This guide covers everything in one place: who can apply, how many stages there are, the full exam pattern, the syllabus, the salary, and how to prepare from scratch.

Everything below is based on the pattern followed in recent WBPSC Clerkship notifications. Details like age limit, fee, qualifying marks and vacancy numbers can change from one notification to the next, so always confirm them in the latest official notification at psc.wb.gov.in before you apply.

The exam at a glance

Point Details
Conducting body West Bengal Public Service Commission (WBPSC)
Posts Lower Division Clerk, Lower Division Assistant and equivalent clerical posts
Minimum qualification Madhyamik (Class 10) pass or equivalent
Age limit 18 to 40 years for general candidates, with relaxation for reserved categories
Selection stages Part I (objective), Part II (written), computer knowledge and typing test
Pay scale Pay Level 6, roughly ₹22,700 to ₹58,500 plus allowances
Job location Within West Bengal
Application mode Online through the official WBPSC website

Eligibility

Educational qualification

You need to have passed the Madhyamik examination of the West Bengal Board of Secondary Education, or an equivalent examination. Higher qualifications like Higher Secondary, graduation or post-graduation are also accepted, since the rule is a minimum. The notification may also mention basic computer knowledge as a requirement, so read that part carefully.

Age limit

In recent notifications, the minimum age is 18 years. The maximum age depends on your category, and it is counted as on a cut-off date mentioned in the notification, not on the day you apply.

Category Minimum age Maximum age (as in recent notifications)
General, and SC/ST/OBC candidates of other states 18 years 40 years
OBC (non-creamy layer) 18 years 43 years
SC/ST of West Bengal, persons with disabilities (PwBD) 18 years 45 years

Other relaxations, such as for ex-servicemen and government employees, are given as per state rules. The notification lists all of them.

Other conditions

You must meet the citizenship, character and medical conditions stated in the notification. You will also need valid documents, like your Madhyamik certificate, caste certificate if applicable, a recent photograph and a signature, at the time of applying and later at document verification.

How many exams are there? The three stages

Many beginners ask how many exams they have to give. The Clerkship selection has three stages, and you have to clear them one after another.

  1. Part I: an objective-type test with multiple choice questions
  2. Part II: a conventional written test in English and a language of your choice
  3. Computer knowledge and typing test: a practical test for those who qualify in both written parts

The final merit list is made from the combined marks of Part I and Part II. The typing test is a qualifying stage, which means you have to pass it, but its marks do not add to your merit score.

Part I: exam pattern

Subject Questions Marks
English 30 30
Arithmetic 30 30
General Studies 40 40
Total 100 100
  • Duration is 90 minutes for the whole paper
  • Each question carries 1 mark
  • Every wrong answer costs 0.25 marks
  • Questions are asked in English and Bengali
  • The paper has multiple choice questions with one correct answer

General Studies carries the most marks, so it has the biggest effect on your Part I score. Arithmetic and English together make up the other 60 marks, and both can be scored well with steady practice.

Part II: exam pattern

Group Subject Marks
Group A English 50
Group B Bengali, Hindi, Urdu, Nepali or Santali (your choice) 50
Total   100 marks in 60 minutes

This is a descriptive paper, so you write your answers by hand, and there is no negative marking. It tests basic writing skills, not literature or deep grammar. The next section explains what is asked in each group.

Computer knowledge and typing test

Candidates who qualify in Part I and Part II are called for a test on elementary computer operation and typing. The typing speeds prescribed in recent notifications are 20 words per minute in English and 10 words per minute in Bengali. This test is qualifying in nature. It is not hard, but plenty of candidates fail it by ignoring it until the last moment, so start practising typing early.

Qualifying marks

You must score a minimum percentage on the combined marks of Part I and Part II to qualify. Recent notifications set it like this.

Category Qualifying marks
Unreserved (General) 40%
EWS 40%
OBC 38%
SC 35%
ST 30%
PwBD 30%
Ex-servicemen 30%
Meritorious sports persons 40%

Qualifying only gets you into the merit list. Your actual rank depends on how many marks you score compared with other candidates, and cut-offs vary from cycle to cycle depending on the difficulty of the paper and the number of vacancies.

Syllabus in detail

The paper is set at the Madhyamik standard. That means you don't need advanced books. If your Class 9 and 10 basics are strong, you already have a head start.

Part I: English (30 marks)

Area Topics to cover
Vocabulary Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitution, idioms and phrases, spelling
Grammar Tenses, articles, prepositions, subject-verb agreement, voice, narration, modals
Sentence work Sentence structure, error spotting, sentence improvement, fill in the blanks

Part I: Arithmetic (30 marks)

Area Topics to cover
Number work Divisibility, fractions, decimals, simplification, LCM and HCF
Ratio and percentage Ratio and proportion, percentage, average, partnership
Money problems Simple interest, profit and loss
Time and motion Time and distance, time and work
Basic geometry Area of rectangles and squares, and simple shapes

Part I: General Studies (40 marks)

Area Topics to cover
Indian history Broad understanding of ancient, medieval and modern India, with the freedom movement
Indian geography Physical features, rivers, climate, resources and agriculture of India
Current events Important national events, with special reference to India, and major world events
Everyday science Basic physics, chemistry and biology, health and daily life science

Questions on West Bengal appear in many state-level exams, so keep a light layer of West Bengal general knowledge on top of this, such as important places, rivers, personalities and recent state news.

Part II: Group A, English (50 marks)

  • Drafting a report in English from the information given
  • Precis writing, which means shortening a passage while keeping its main points
  • Translation from Bengali, Hindi, Urdu, Nepali or Santali into English

Part II: Group B, your chosen language (50 marks)

  • Drafting a report in the chosen language
  • Precis writing in the chosen language
  • Translation from English into the chosen language
The exact tasks in Part II can be worded a little differently in each notification. Check the syllabus section of the latest advertisement for the final list.

Salary and benefits

Clerks in West Bengal are placed at Pay Level 6 of the state pay structure, with a scale of roughly ₹22,700 to ₹58,500. The starting basic pay is at the lower end of that range, and it grows with annual increments and promotions.

On top of basic pay you get Dearness Allowance, House Rent Allowance, medical benefits and other admissible allowances. DA and HRA rates are decided by the state government and can change, so your in-hand salary depends on the rates in force at the time and the city where you are posted. Deductions like contributions towards pension or provident fund and professional tax come off before you receive it.

The pay is modest at the start, but the job comes with security, regular increments, leave and pension-related benefits, and a clear promotion path. That is why so many people prefer it over uncertain private jobs.

The job and career growth

As a clerk, your work is mostly office work: handling files and notes, maintaining records, drafting letters, entering data on computers, dealing with public queries at a counter in some offices, and helping senior officers with day-to-day paperwork. Postings are within West Bengal, in the Secretariat in Kolkata, directorates, or district and regional offices.

Promotions generally move from clerk to higher clerical and assistant posts and then to supervisory posts, through seniority and departmental exams. The speed varies by department, so treat your starting post as one you will hold for a good while. Vacancies are sometimes announced after the application stage, and appointments may start on a temporary basis under the rules of the notification.

How to prepare for the Clerkship exam

Since the level is Madhyamik, your preparation should be built on basics and speed, not on heavy books. Here is a simple way to split your time.

Subject Marks How to prepare
General Studies 40 Read school textbooks of Class 6 to 10 for history, geography and science. Read a newspaper daily and keep short notes on current events
Arithmetic 30 Learn tables, squares and basic formulas first. Then practise topic by topic with a timer, and revisit mistakes
English 30 Study grammar rules from a simple book, build vocabulary daily, and solve error spotting and fill-in-the-blank sets
Part II writing 100 Write one short report, precis and translation each week from the start, in both English and your chosen language
Typing Qualifying Practise English and Bengali typing for 20 to 30 minutes a day, since the required speed is low but needs practice

A simple study order

  1. Start with the syllabus and a few previous year papers to see the level of questions
  2. Spend the first month on basics: arithmetic fundamentals, grammar and school textbook reading
  3. In the next phase, practise topic-wise questions every day and keep a notebook of mistakes
  4. Start Part II writing early, because handwriting speed and clear drafting take months to build
  5. In the last phase, take full-length Part I mocks and revise your notes
  6. Do not leave typing practice for the end

Part I strategy that works

With 0.25 negative marking, blind guessing hurts. If you can remove two options with confidence, a guess is usually fine. If you have no idea, skip it. Do the sections you are strongest in first, and keep General Studies for a calm moment, since it is quick if you know the topic and a waste of time if you don't. Practise finishing a full paper in 90 minutes, with a few minutes left to review.

Part II strategy that works

For the report and the precis, plain sentences are enough. Nobody is checking for fancy words. Have a clear start and finish, and keep to the word limit. In translation, get the meaning across correctly instead of converting every word one by one, because that usually gives you awkward sentences. And keep an eye on the clock while you practise. Sixty minutes for two languages disappears fast, and it is easy to run out of time on the second group.

Where people usually slip

The biggest slip is taking the exam lightly because the level is Madhyamik. The questions are simple, but lakhs of people are solving the same simple questions, and a few marks decide the rank. Part II comes next. Many people wait for the Part I result and only then start writing, and by that time there is hardly any room to fix their handwriting speed or their drafting.

Typing gets ignored too, since it feels like a formality. It isn't one. It is a qualifying stage, and you can't be selected without clearing it. A few smaller things also cost marks: reading five books instead of revising one properly, never looking at the mistakes in your mock tests, guessing too much in Part I, and getting documents or details wrong during the application and verification.

Common questions

Can graduates apply for the Clerkship exam?

Yes. Madhyamik is only the minimum, so graduates and post-graduates can apply too. They just have to fit the age limit and the other conditions in the notification.

Is there an interview?

Not in the process described in recent notifications. Your selection depends on the Part I and Part II marks, and after that you have to clear the computer and typing test.

Do I have to know Bengali?

Not for Part II, because you can pick Hindi, Urdu, Nepali or Santali instead. The typing test is different, since it has a Bengali typing requirement. Check how the notification words it for your case.

Does the exam come every year?

No, there is no fixed yearly schedule. The gap between two notifications can be long, and nobody outside the commission knows the date beforehand. So don't wait for the advertisement to start. People who begin only after it comes out usually find the time too short.

How long does preparation take?

If your basics are decent, four to six months of regular daily study is a reasonable target. If you have been out of studies for years, or you are starting from nothing, plan for more.

Is there negative marking in Part II?

No. The 0.25 deduction is only for wrong answers in the objective Part I.

Final word

The WBPSC Clerkship exam rewards people who prepare the basics well and stay consistent. The syllabus is at the Madhyamik level, the pattern is simple, and the three stages are easy to understand. What separates those who get selected from those who don't is mostly practice: timed arithmetic sets, regular writing for Part II, a daily newspaper habit, and a bit of typing every day. Start with the official syllabus, make a simple plan, and keep checking the official site for the latest notification.
